sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Liberalisation**: Abolition of industrial licensing except for a short list of strategic/hazardous sectors, removal of capacity constraints, freedom to fix prices, and reduction in **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** and **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)**.
• **Privatisation**: Transfer of ownership, management, or control of public sector enterprises (PSEs) to the private sector through **Disinvestment**, strategic sale, and opening up reserved sectors.
• **Globalisation**: Integration of the national economy with the world economy through the removal of trade barriers, reduction of import tariffs, full convertibility on the current account, and welcoming **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)**.
• **Key Trigger / Catalyst**: The severe **1991 Balance of Payments crisis**, where India's foreign exchange reserves plummeted to less than $1.2 billion (barely enough for 2 weeks of essential imports) forcing emergency gold pledging to the Bank of England and IMF conditionalities.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Short-term measures (1991-92) aimed at correcting weaknesses in the Balance of Payments and controlling inflation.
Controlling government expenditure, devaluation of the rupee, and tightening monetary policy.
Often confused with structural reforms in Prelims statements.
Long-term policies designed to improve economic efficiency, increase international competitiveness, and remove rigidities.
Industrial de-licensing, trade policy liberalization, financial sector reforms, and tax reforms.
Core focus area for Mains GS-3 questions on economic development.
First Generation vs Second Generation Reforms
First Gen (1991 onwards): Industries, trade, exchange rates, foreign investment. Second Gen (Late 1990s/2000s): Factor markets, legal systems, public sector governance, administrative reforms.
Evolution from crisis-driven fire-fighting to institutional strengthening and long-term sustainable growth.
Distinction frequently tested in analytical MCQs.

items.definition: The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act was scrapped and replaced by the Competition Act, 2002 to shift focus from curbing monopoly size to preventing anti-competitive practices and abuse of dominance.

Disinvestment is the sale of a portion of government equity in PSUs (keeping majority stake), whereas Privatisation involves handing over management control and majority ownership to private entities.
Introduced in 1994 (accepting Article VIII of IMF), allowing free conversion of rupee into foreign currency and vice versa for current international transactions (trade, services, interest).
Narasimham Committee (Financial Sector Reforms), Raja Chellaiah Committee (Tax Reforms), Rangarajan Committee (Disinvestment), and Abid Hussain Committee (Small Scale Industries).

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution & Sectoral Impact
items.content:
• **Service Sector Hubs**: Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Gurugram, Pune, and Chennai emerged as global IT, ITeS, and financial service capitals due to liberalized telecom and FDI policies.
• **Regional Disparities**: Coastal and southern states attracted higher FDI and industrial growth post-1991, while hinterland agrarian states witnessed slower structural transformation, creating regional divergence.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: 'Jobless growth', agrarian distress, rising economic inequality, informal sector vulnerability, and non-performing assets (NPAs) in banking.
• **Policy Interventions**: Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP), Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), and targeted welfare digitalization (JAM Trinity).

items.title: Mnemonic for Core Reform Committees
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "Narasimham drives Finance, Chellaiah counts Taxes, Rangarajan sells Shares."
• **Decoded Meaning**: Narasimham Committee = Financial Sector Reforms; Raja Chellaiah Committee = Tax Reforms; Rangarajan Committee = Disinvestment.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly matches committees to their respective reform domains without confusion.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Remember the twin pillars of 1991: Stabilisation (Short-term BoP/Inflation control) came *before* Structural Reforms (Long-term market efficiency).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often states that 'India adopted full Capital Account Convertibility in 1991.' This is completely false. India only achieved Current Account Convertibility in 1994; Capital Account Convertibility remains partially restricted (governed by Tarapore Committee recommendations).

Mains Value Addition: Use the phrase 'From Licence-Permit-Quota Raj to Ease of Doing Business' in your introduction. Conclude with structural shifts toward 'Atmanirbhar Bharat' (Self-Reliant India) balanced with global integration ('Global Value Chains').

keyTakeaways: The 1991 LPG strategy was a structural paradigm shift from state-led import substitution to market-driven export orientation.
Stabilisation policies tackled immediate macroeconomic imbalances, while structural reforms permanently transformed industrial, financial, and trade landscapes.
While LPG unlocked high GDP growth and global integration, it necessitated subsequent policy corrections to address regional disparities, agricultural stagnation, and informal sector vulnerabilities.
